processing: Made as other raw pu-erh is: large-leaf spring tea is pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried into maocha, then sold loose or pressed without any ripening pile.
harvest_season: As usual across Yiwu, spring is the prized picking, with lesser summer and autumn lots.
appearance_dry: Broad, thick, dark-green leaves, usually pressed into a cake.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden yellow, fairly deep in colour.
appearance_wet: Broad, thick large leaves that open supple and dark olive green.
taste_profile: A high, sweet aroma over the soft body Yiwu is known for, with a quick, lively return of sweetness and moisture in the mouth.

brewing.notes: Rinse briefly. A gaiwan shows the aroma well; shorten the steeps if a young cake turns sharp.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year like other raw pu-erh, with spring lots at the top. Village-named cakes are mostly recent vintages drunk young or stored for years, and older ones are rare under this name. One published spring price list put it at 900 to 1000 yuan per kilo for maocha, which gives a rough idea of its standing but dates quickly.
description:
Sanheshe is a Yi village in the Yiwu tea area of southern Yunnan, counted among the seven villages in the local shorthand "seven villages, eight hamlets". It sits across a river from the old gardens of Mahei, and its trees grow among forest trees in a well-kept landscape.

Processing follows the raw pu-erh pattern: pan-firing, rolling and sun-drying, then pressing or not. Nothing about the method is particular to this village, so the character comes from the leaf and the place.

The leaves are described as broad, thick and dark green, brewing to a clear golden liquor. Expect a high, sweet aroma and a fast return of sweetness rather than heavy bitterness. As with other Yiwu teas, it rewards short steeps with very hot water.

The name appears in several spellings, San He Zhai among them, so check that a seller really means this village. Ask for the harvest year and season, and remember that a village name on a wrapper is hard to verify from the outside.
history: Sanheshe is described as a long-settled tea-growing Yi village, but little is documented about when its gardens were planted or who first sold its tea under the village name. Its place in the tea world today comes from the "seven villages, eight hamlets" grouping used for Yiwu.
